questions.q: Which way does a comet's tail point, and does that change when the comet is moving away from the Sun?
questions.do: In the Orbit player, pick Halley and press Play. Watch the tail before and after the comet passes the Sun.
questions.a: The tail always points away from the Sun. After the comet goes round the Sun it travels out tail first, because sunlight and the solar wind push the gas and dust outward, whichever way the comet is moving.

questions.q: How fast was 3I/ATLAS moving at its closest point to the Sun, and why will it never come back?
questions.do: Tap 3I/ATLAS, drag the time slider until it says closest to the Sun, and read Speed. Then read the path shape under the comet's facts.
questions.a: About 68 km/s (roughly 246,000 km/h). Its path shape number is e = 6.1, far above 1, so its path is an open curve: it came from another star, passes the Sun once and leaves for ever.

questions.q: At 3 au from the Sun, sunlight is about 1/9 as strong as at Earth. How much slower does water ice turn to gas there than at 1 au?
questions.do: In Why the tail grows, set the slider to 3.00 au and read Ice to gas vs 1 au.
questions.a: About 1/590, hundreds of times slower, even though the sunlight is only 9 times weaker. That is why comets usually switch on only inside about 3 au.

questions.q: Who first spotted Halley's Comet on its predicted return, and when?
questions.a: Johann Palitzsch, a German farmer and amateur astronomer, on 25 December 1758. Halley had predicted the return in 1705 but had died in 1742. The comet passed the Sun on 13 March 1759.

questions.q: Using only the Sun's pull, when would Halley next come closest to the Sun? How does that compare with JPL's answer?
questions.do: Open Checks and read the last row of the table.
questions.a: The page's Sun-only calculation says about 11 Feb 2062; JPL, which adds the pull of Jupiter, Saturn and the other planets, says 28 July 2061, about 198 days earlier. The planets' tugs matter over a whole orbit.
